transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-09-14 17:00 UTC | Duration: ~64 minutes | Recorded on Fireflies
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Avery Lin (TemporalCore Head of Cloud Partnerships), Marko Petrovic (TemporalCore Infra Lead), Lena Suarez (BizDev), Omar Rizvi (Security)

Summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and TemporalCore. Covered deployment models, routing/failover, security (KMS, SOC2), benchmarking approach and next steps to run a joint pilot. Action items assigned.

00:00:08 Jordan Mills: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros -- i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the partner motion. Priya and Ethan from our solutions engineering team are with me.
00:00:20 Avery Lin: Hi all, Avery from TemporalCore, thanks for taking the time. Marko, Lena, and Omar are on the call. We're exploring a tighter channel partnership, want to understand integration effort for our cloud GPU offering.
00:00:35 Priya Kapoor: Great, thanks Avery. Today we wanna cover three things: how we integrate end-to-end (api + routing), security guardrails for enterprise customers, and a pilot/benchmark plan so your customers can validate performance vs cost.
00:00:48 Marko Petrovic: Sounds good. Very interested in the dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, and how we can route to TemporalCore nodes when customers pick your platform in our marketplace.
00:01:05 Ethan Cho: To frame it -- Redwood offers hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and a private deployment option (VPC/on-prem). For a marketplace use-case you mentioned, we typically see either dedicated pools for resellers or a VPC-private control plane integration. Both have different network and auth implications.
00:01:30 Lena Suarez: Our marketplace goal is giving customers predictable latency and predictable billing. Some enterprise customers will want data to never leave their org or region.
00:01:44 Jordan Mills: Totally — that's where our private deployment and key management integrations come in. Omar, any specific security or compliance questions up front?
00:01:55 Omar Rizvi: Yes — we need to assess KMS/HSM integration, audit log fidelity (request-level tracing), and encryption in flight and at rest. Also SSO for admin controls, RBAC mapping for tenant isolation. Do you have SOC2 artifacts to share?
00:02:14 Priya Kapoor: We do. We can share SOC2 type II reports and our security pack. Quick note: our private deployments support customer-managed KMS integrations and generate per-request audit logs; we can correlate tokens to tenant ids for auditability.
00:02:32 Marko Petrovic: When you say 'audit logs' is the granularity down to individual request payloads or just metadata? We need payload-level correlation for certain regulated customers.
00:02:45 Priya Kapoor: Good clarif. By default logs capture metadata, latencies, token counts, and request identifiers. Sensitive payloads are redacted by default; if a customer has a retention exception we can enable additional logging under contract and with encryption-at-rest plus restricted KMS keys. That's a legal/compliance conversation.
00:03:10 Avery Lin: Ok that helps. On the routing side — we need to know how Redwood's smart routing would pick between a TemporalCore-backed GPU pool vs Redwood-hosted model. E.g., cost driven vs latency driven policies.
00:03:25 Ethan Cho: Our smart routing supports policy layers: prefer low-latency region, fall back to cost-optimized model variant, or explicit force route to partner capacity. We also have automatic fallback rules so if your pool is saturated, requests go to a compatible model variant elsewhere.
00:03:47 Jordan Mills: For marketplace integration, we can expose a routing tag so your customers can select 'TemporalCore GPU' and then our router ensures requests go to your capacity when available, otherwise it shows a capacity warning and can route to a Redwood-verified fallback.
00:04:03 Marko Petrovic: Is that routing synchronous? We need sub-50ms extra overhead ideally.
00:04:12 Priya Kapoor: Routing decision is done at the control plane level and we cache routing for opened sessions; typical overhead is low single-digit ms in the control plane, bulk of latency is the first token/generation time. We can share our latency profs.
00:04:25 Avery Lin: Nice. Let's talk about KV cache and prefix caching. A lot of our customers will run chat assistants that benefit from large KV caches. How does Redwood manage KV caching across partner pools?
00:04:40 Ethan Cho: We keep an active KV cache on the serving nodes. When requests route to TemporalCore GPUs, the cache is hot on those nodes. For cross-pool routing (e.g., fallback to Redwood host), we persist KV cache snapshots and can warm them on the target pool, but there's a warm-up delta. For strict latency SLAs, we recommend pinning sessions to the same pool.
00:05:05 Marko Petrovic: Important — pinning to our pool is fine, but what happens when autoscaling adds more GPUs? Does the KV cache migrate?
00:05:15 Priya Kapoor: Autoscaling creates new nodes; we use a distributed KV replicate and warm-up strategy. It's not transparent zero-cost migration — there are short tail effects. Quantifyable in a benchmark; we'll include this in the pilot matrix.
00:05:30 Lena Suarez: From a commercial perspective, how do billing and credits work if a customer uses TemporalCore CPU/GPU plus Redwood API? We want a clean flow.
00:05:42 Jordan Mills: We typically support partner billing via an integration where usage records include tags for partner capacity. The marketplace operator (you) gets a consolidated view and we can emit partner-specific billing events. We also support committed reserved capacity for predictable pricing.
00:06:00 Avery Lin: Ok cool. Next — sample workloads. We'll share concurrency and sequences. Marko: our typical inference workload is a mix — 60% chat-like (avg seq 350 tokens), 30% embedding and rerank, 10% long-form generation for internal tooling. P95 latency target for chat is 250ms at baseline.
00:06:26 Marko Petrovic: Yes we should be explicit: 250ms P95 for 95% of calls at concurrency ~2k user sessions, burst to 5k.
00:06:37 Priya Kapoor: That is helpful. We will dimension the pilot test to emulate that concurrency and sequence distribution. For 250ms P95 we'd likely recommend an FP16-optimized model or a quantized variant depending on model family — we can propose three model knobs in the recommendation.
00:06:55 Ethan Cho: We'll also include batching parameters and recommended max batch size, dynamic batching window, and a breakdown of per-token cost across the routing choices.
00:07:07 Omar Rizvi: On encryption — if we integrate our KMS, does Redwood accept bring-your-own-key for models served on your hosted infrastructure?
00:07:18 Priya Kapoor: For hosted API, BYOK isn't available today — hosted uses Redwood-managed encryption; for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (BYOK) and HSM-backed flows. We can note this in the security pack.
00:07:33 Jordan Mills: If your customers require strict BYOK we recommend the private deployment path or a co-deploy model.
00:07:41 Lena Suarez: From an integration effort standpoint, what is the typical timeline to go from kickoff to a marketplace listing? We're aiming for a Q4 enablement window, two months ideally.
00:07:55 Jordan Mills: Typical timeline 6–8 weeks for a basic integration (API + routing + brief security review) — 8–12 weeks if you need private deployment and additional compliance reviews. We can fast-track some steps if both teams commit resources.
00:08:10 Avery Lin: Ok. Let's dig a bit into the technical pieces — can you outline the API surface we'd need to call for routing and submitting jobs?
00:08:22 Priya Kapoor: Sure. High-level: a single REST endpoint for generation and embeddings with model IDs; a routing control API to register partner pools and health checks; and a handshake for per-request tokens and tenant mapping. We'll send the API spec after this meeting.
00:08:39 Ethan Cho: Also, for persistent sessions we expose a session endpoint which keeps KV handles and avoids re-sending the full context on each request, useful for chat-heavy workloads.
00:08:50 Marko Petrovic: Would session handles be transferable across pools? We heard about warm-up; but does the handle include KV pointers or includes content?
00:09:02 Priya Kapoor: Session handles reference server-side KV caches. If you move pools, you need to warm the cache. We can provide snapshot/restore endpoints which allow you to serialize a session's KV and restore it on a target pool — but that has time and cost.
00:09:20 Lena Suarez: That snapshot/restore flow could be productized in the marketplace listing as an advanced feature.
00:09:28 Jordan Mills: Agreed, we can design an 'enterprise' listing tier that includes session pinning and KMS integration.
00:09:36 Avery Lin: On the operational side — we need per-tenant observability. What level of telemetry do you provide to partners?
00:09:46 Priya Kapoor: We provide token-level breakdowns, latency histograms per route, model-level dashboards, and tracing hooks. For partners we can open a partner view that shows a filtered lens into only partner assets and usage.
00:10:00 Omar Rizvi: Are there any data retention defaults? Some customers need 90-day retention; others need 7 years for audits.
00:10:09 Priya Kapoor: Default retention is 90 days for logs and 30 days for request payloads (redacted). We can extend retention under contract for private deployments.
00:10:20 Marko Petrovic: Ok. Switching to benchmarking — what would you like from us to run a realistic bench?
00:10:28 Ethan Cho: We'll need a representative payload set (chat turns, embedding sizes, rerank batch sizes), concurrency targets, burst profiles, and any network constraints (e.g., customers in APAC with higher RTT). Also list of model families you'd like tested.
00:10:45 Marko Petrovic: We'll prepare that. We'll also provide a staging API key and access to one of our test GPU pools.
00:10:52 Jordan Mills: Great. We'll propose a 2-week pilot that includes baseline runs, a peak concurrency run, and a long-duration stability run. We'll produce a matrix showing P50/P95/P99 and cost per 1k requests.
00:11:07 Avery Lin: Sounds good. A question on SLAs: do you offer uptime and latency SLAs for partner offerings?
00:11:17 Priya Kapoor: For Redwood Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; for hosted we have best-effort and a published reliability profile. Private deployments can include custom SLA in the contract.
00:11:30 Jordan Mills: For marketplace co-sells, we often recommend Dedicated for enterprise customers who need SLAs and Private for the most sensitive workloads.
00:11:40 Lena Suarez: On the commercial side, if a joint customer uses TemporalCore capacity via Redwood API, what's the revenue split model look like?
00:11:50 Jordan Mills: We typically work out revenue-share agreements per partnership. The marketplace operator gets a margin on capacity usage and we handle the API. We'll set up a commercial working group after this call to draft terms.
00:12:05 Avery Lin: Good. Any red flags or blockers we should be aware of now?
00:12:10 Priya Kapoor: From a product side, the two things to watch are BYOK availability on hosted and session migration warm-up costs. Both are solvable but affect commercial/ops decisions.
00:12:22 Omar Rizvi: From security, we want to validate KMS key separation and ensure audit log immutability for regulated customers. Also need to understand where metadata is stored globally.
00:12:34 Jordan Mills: We'll include those items in the security pack and have Priya follow up with a technical appendix.
00:12:40 Ethan Cho: Quick note — does TemporalCore have a preferred model set? Are you onboarding any open-model variants we should optimize for?
00:12:48 Marko Petrovic: We're running a mix: Llama-family variants for embeddings and a couple of transformer families for chat. We'll detail exact model names in the workload doc.
00:12:58 Lena Suarez: We're also exploring quantized builds to reduce cost. Would Redwood support multiple quantization profiles per model?
00:13:06 Priya Kapoor: Yes, we support multiple profiles and can recommend quantization levels per workload. We also monitor quality regressions through eval sets.
00:13:15 Jordan Mills: To wrap up before we go into scheduling — recap of next steps: Jordan will send integration deck and quickstart; Priya and Ethan will sketch benchmark matrix; TemporalCore to share workload profile and staging access; Omar and Priya will exchange security docs.
00:13:32 Avery Lin: That's correct. Quick scheduling question: can you run a 2-hour technical deep-dive + pilot planning session next Wednesday (2027-09-22) with our infra team?
00:13:44 Jordan Mills: We have availability — we'll follow up with a Doodle.
00:13:50 Marko Petrovic: Minor note, please include an ops checklist for agents and routing health checks so our SREs can onboard faster.
00:13:58 Ethan Cho: We'll include a step-by-step ops checklist and a sample health-check dashboard in the repo.
00:14:06 Lena Suarez: Great. One more question — competitors. Some customers ask how Redwood compares to Aurora Compute and others. Any quick bullet points?
00:14:17 Jordan Mills: Short version: our focus is production-first inference with unified serving across hosted/dedicated/private, deeper observability, and cost controls (batching, cache). We'll send a one-pager comparing top competitors.
00:14:30 Avery Lin: Perfect. Anything else?
00:14:34 Priya Kapoor: Nothing else from Redwood. Thanks everyone.
00:14:37 Jordan Mills: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the bench planning session.
00:14:44 Meeting end.
